entities.name: Epistle to the Galatians
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Epistle to the Galatians is a foundational New Testament text attributed to Paul the Apostle, written circa 55-65 CE. This influential letter addresses issues of Christian identity, Jewish law, and the role of Gentile Christians in the early Church, shaping the trajectory of Western Christianity.





The Epistle to the Galatians is part of the Pauline corpus, a collection of letters attributed to Paul that span his missionary journeys. The letter's significance lies in its assertion of Christian universalism, which countered the strictures of Jewish law and welcomed Gentiles into the fold of Christianity.




The Epistle to the Galatians has had a lasting impact on Western Christianity, influencing the development of theology, liturgy, and ecclesiology. Its themes of inclusivity, grace, and love have resonated across centuries, shaping the lives of countless believers.




In the words of Paul himself, 'I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes' (Galatians 2:8).
